title: Crypto Funding Complete Guide
subtitle: Master Web3 Funding from Grants to Venture Capital

intro.title: Introduction to Crypto Funding
intro.content:
Funding in crypto works fundamentally differently than traditional finance. Instead of pitching banks or conventional VCs who may not understand blockchain technology, you have access to a thriving ecosystem of crypto-native funding sources—from permissionless grants to specialized VCs who deeply understand your space.

In this comprehensive guide, you'll learn about every major funding path in crypto: ecosystem grants, quadratic funding, retroactive public goods funding, venture capital, token sales, and community funding. We'll cover real examples, application strategies, and how to build the relationships that lead to successful fundraising.

funding_types.title: Types of Crypto Funding
funding_types.content: Understanding the crypto funding landscape is your first step. Unlike traditional finance with limited options, crypto offers diverse funding mechanisms, each suited for different project stages and goals.

grants.title: Grants
grants.content:
Grants are non-dilutive funding (no equity given up) typically focused on public goods, infrastructure, and ecosystem development. They're often the best starting point for early-stage projects.

Key characteristics:

  • Non-dilutive: No equity or tokens required
  • Milestone-based: Funding released based on deliverables
  • Public goods focus: Prefer projects benefiting the ecosystem
  • Amounts: Typically $5K-$500K, some larger programs up to $1M+

Best for:

  • Open-source infrastructure and tools
  • Research and education
  • Developer tooling and libraries
  • Community building initiatives
  • Standards and documentation

Not ideal for: Revenue-focused businesses, closed-source projects, or those requiring large capital for go-to-market.

venture_capital.title: Venture Capital
venture_capital.content:
Crypto VCs invest in high-growth projects in exchange for equity (in a company) or tokens (in a protocol). They provide capital, connections, and strategic guidance.

Funding rounds:

  • Pre-seed: $500K-$2M, idea to early product
  • Seed: $2M-$10M, product-market fit exploration
  • Series A: $10M-$30M, scaling proven model
  • Series B+: $30M+, market leadership and expansion

What VCs look for:

  • Team: Exceptional founders with relevant experience
  • Market: Large addressable market, clear pain point
  • Traction: User growth, TVL, revenue, or network effects
  • Token economics: Well-designed value accrual and incentives
  • Differentiation: Unique approach or unfair advantage

Top crypto VCs: a16z Crypto, Paradigm, Polychain, Pantera, Multicoin, Dragonfly, Framework Ventures, Electric Capital, Variant.

crowdfunding.title: Crowdfunding & Token Sales
crowdfunding.content:
Crowdfunding lets you raise capital directly from your community, either through platforms or token sales. This maintains community ownership and alignment.

Models:

  • Juicebox: Ethereum-native crowdfunding with NFT rewards
  • Token sales (IDO/IEO): Sell tokens to early supporters
  • Public sale via launchpads: Use platforms like CoinList
  • Fair launch: No pre-sale, everyone gets same price

Advantages:

  • Build engaged community from day one
  • Maintain decentralization and community ownership
  • Faster than VC fundraising process
  • Demonstrate market demand

Challenges:

  • Regulatory complexity (especially in US)
  • Requires existing community and trust
  • High expectations from token holders
  • Token price volatility creates pressure

retroactive_funding.title: Retroactive Public Goods Funding
retroactive_funding.content:
Retroactive funding is a paradigm shift: instead of predicting which projects will succeed, fund them after they've proven impact. This rewards builders who deliver value to the ecosystem.

How it works:

  1. Build and ship a public good
  2. Demonstrate impact to the community
  3. Get nominated for retroactive funding round
  4. Badgeholders or voters decide allocation
  5. Receive funding based on past impact

Optimism RetroPGF: The largest retroactive funding program, distributing millions in OP tokens across rounds:

  • RetroPGF 1 (2021): $1M to 58 projects
  • RetroPGF 2 (2023): 10M OP (~$10M) to 195 projects
  • RetroPGF 3 (2023): 30M OP (~$30M) to 643 projects
  • RetroPGF 4 (2024+): Ongoing iterations

Strategy: Don't wait for grants—build valuable public goods now, document impact, and participate in retroactive rounds when announced.

grant_programs.title: Major Grant Programs
grant_programs.content: Crypto grant programs distribute hundreds of millions of dollars annually. Understanding each program's focus and application process is key to success.

ethereum_foundation.title: Ethereum Foundation Grants
ethereum_foundation.content:
The Ethereum Foundation's Ecosystem Support Program (ESP) is one of the most prestigious grant programs, funding core infrastructure, research, and community initiatives.

Focus areas:

  • Core protocol: Client diversity, consensus research, EVM improvements
  • Developer tooling: Testing frameworks, debugging tools, IDEs
  • Cryptography & security: ZKP research, audits, formal verification
  • Education & community: Documentation, translations, local communities
  • Applied research: Scalability, privacy, MEV solutions

Grant sizes: Typically $50K-$500K, can be higher for critical infrastructure.

Application process:

  1. Submit inquiry via Ethereum Foundation website
  2. Initial review (2-4 weeks)
  3. Detailed proposal if promising
  4. Due diligence and interviews
  5. Funding decision and milestone setup

Success tips:

  • Align with Ethereum roadmap (The Surge, Scourge, Verge, Purge, Splurge)
  • Demonstrate technical capability and relevant experience
  • Show clear deliverables and timeline
  • Emphasize public good nature and open-source commitment

gitcoin.title: Gitcoin Grants
gitcoin.content:
Gitcoin pioneered quadratic funding for open-source crypto projects. Instead of a committee deciding, community donations are matched by a pool using quadratic matching.

How quadratic funding works:

  • You donate to projects you support
  • Matching pool amplifies small donations more than large ones
  • $1 from 100 people gets more matching than $100 from 1 person
  • Formula: Match = (√d₁ + √d₂ + √d₃...)² where d = donation

Example: Project A gets $100 from 1 donor = $10 match. Project B gets $10 from 10 donors = $100 match. This favors projects with broad community support over whale-funded projects.

Grant rounds:

  • Main rounds: Quarterly, $100K-$2M matching pools
  • Ecosystem rounds: Specific to chains (Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum)
  • Thematic rounds: DeFi, climate, DEI, etc.

Grants Stack: Gitcoin's new protocol allows anyone to run their own quadratic funding rounds.

Success strategy:

  • Build community before the round starts
  • Create compelling project page with clear impact
  • Engage actively during the round
  • Show ongoing development and transparency

optimism_retropgf.title: Optimism RetroPGF
optimism_retropgf.content:
Optimism's Retroactive Public Goods Funding (RetroPGF) rewards projects that have already delivered value to the Optimism ecosystem and Ethereum as a whole.

What's funded:

  • Infrastructure: RPC providers, indexers, oracles
  • Developer tools: Libraries, frameworks, educational content
  • Applications: DeFi, NFTs, governance tools
  • Community: Educational content, translations, events

Process:

  1. Nominations: Anyone can nominate projects (or self-nominate)
  2. Applications: Projects submit impact descriptions
  3. Evaluation: Badgeholders (selected community members) review
  4. Voting: Badgeholders allocate their budget across projects
  5. Distribution: OP tokens distributed based on votes

RetroPGF 3 results (30M OP):

  • 643 projects funded
  • Median: ~14K OP (~$30K)
  • Top projects: 400K-500K OP ($800K-$1M)
  • Categories: Infrastructure (40%), Tools (30%), Community (20%), Other (10%)

Key insight: RetroPGF rewards proven impact over promises. Build something valuable, document your impact clearly, and you'll be rewarded retroactively.

ecosystem_grants.title: Ecosystem-Specific Grants
ecosystem_grants.content:
Every major blockchain ecosystem runs grant programs to fund applications, infrastructure, and community initiatives on their chain.

Arbitrum Grants:

  • Focus: DeFi, gaming, social, infrastructure
  • Amounts: $10K-$500K
  • ARB token grants from DAO treasury
  • Governance via Arbitrum DAO

Polygon Grants:

  • Focus: Gaming, DeFi, NFTs, social, ZK applications
  • Village program: incubation + funding
  • Amounts: $5K-$1M depending on stage

Solana Grants:

  • Focus: DeFi, gaming, mobile, payments
  • Developer grants: tools and infrastructure
  • Integration grants: bringing projects to Solana

Protocol-specific grants:

  • Uniswap Grants: UNI DAO grants for ecosystem tools
  • Aave Grants: AGD funds Aave ecosystem development
  • Compound Grants: COMP grants for governance, tools, integrations

Strategy: If you're building on a specific chain, apply to that ecosystem's grants. Often easier than competing for general Ethereum grants.

vc_landscape.title: The Crypto VC Landscape
vc_landscape.content: Crypto venture capital has evolved into a sophisticated ecosystem with specialized firms, each with unique investment theses and value propositions.

crypto_vcs.title: Major Crypto VCs
crypto_vcs.content:
Understanding different VCs helps you target the right partners for your project stage and focus area.

Tier 1 - Largest funds ($1B+):

  • a16z Crypto: $7.6B across funds, broad portfolio, strong regulatory advocacy
  • Paradigm: $13B+ AUM, research-focused, large positions, technical depth
  • Polychain: Pioneer crypto VC, thesis-driven, protocol investments
  • Pantera: Oldest crypto fund (2013), broad crypto exposure

Thesis-driven VCs:

  • Multicoin Capital: Strongly opinionated theses (Web3, Solana ecosystem)
  • Dragonfly: Cross-border (US/Asia), infrastructure and DeFi
  • Variant: Ownership economy, consumer crypto, creator economy

Stage-specific:

  • Framework Ventures: Early-stage DeFi and gaming
  • Electric Capital: Developer ecosystem focus, publishes dev reports
  • Placeholder: Early-stage networks and protocols

Corporate VCs:

  • Coinbase Ventures: 300+ portfolio companies, strategic alignment
  • Binance Labs: Focus on projects using BNB Chain, incubation
  • Galaxy Digital: Mike Novogratz's firm, institutional focus

Geographic specialization:

  • HashKey Capital: Asia focus, Hong Kong-based, regulatory expertise
  • Spartan Group: Asia-focused, advisory services
  • LongHash Ventures: Asia accelerator + VC

deal_terms.title: Understanding VC Deal Terms
deal_terms.content:
Crypto VC deals have unique structures compared to traditional venture. Understanding these terms is crucial for negotiation.

Investment structures:

  • SAFT (Simple Agreement for Future Tokens): Promise to deliver tokens at launch, common for pre-token projects
  • Token purchase: Direct purchase of tokens at discount to future public price
  • Equity: Traditional equity in the company (less common in pure protocol plays)
  • Hybrid: Both equity and tokens

Key terms to negotiate:

  • Valuation: Fully diluted valuation (FDV) vs market cap
  • Vesting: Typically 4 years with 1-year cliff for team; VCs often get shorter vests
  • Lock-up: Period after TGE before VC can sell (6-24 months typical)
  • Linear vs cliff: Linear release (monthly) vs cliff (quarterly/yearly)
  • Discount: VCs typically get 20-50% discount to public sale price
  • Pro-rata rights: Right to maintain ownership % in future rounds

Red flags:

  • No lock-up (VC can dump immediately after launch)
  • Excessive allocation (>20% to VCs creates overhang)
  • Control provisions (VCs shouldn't control decentralized protocols)
  • Unfavorable token economics (team/community get too little)

valuations.title: Crypto Valuations
valuations.content:
Crypto valuations are art + science, often based on comparable protocols, growth metrics, and token economics.

Valuation methods:

  • Comparable multiples: Look at similar projects' FDV/TVL, FDV/revenue, FDV/users
  • Network value: Metcalfe's law (value proportional to users²)
  • DCF (Discounted Cash Flow): Project future revenue/fees and discount to present
  • Stage-based: Pre-seed $5-20M, Seed $20-100M, A $100-500M, B+ $500M+

DeFi protocol valuations:

  • High TVL (>$1B): 0.3-1.5x TVL for FDV is reasonable
  • Growing revenue: 10-50x annualized revenue for high-growth
  • Strong token economics: Premium for protocols with real yield and buybacks

Market cycles matter:

  • Bull market (2021): Seed rounds at $100-500M FDV common
  • Bear market (2022-2023): Same stage at $20-50M FDV
  • Recovery (2024+): Valuations recovering but more rational

Typical allocations:

  • Team: 15-25%
  • Investors: 15-30%
  • Treasury/DAO: 30-50%
  • Community/ecosystem: 20-40%

crowdfunding.title: Crowdfunding & Community Funding
crowdfunding.content: Crowdfunding in crypto allows you to raise from your community while maintaining alignment and decentralization.

juicebox.title: Juicebox Protocol
juicebox.content:
Juicebox is an Ethereum-native crowdfunding platform where projects can raise ETH and distribute governance tokens or NFTs to supporters.

How it works:

  1. Create a project and set funding goals/terms
  2. Contributors send ETH to your project
  3. They receive project tokens or NFTs
  4. You can set overflow (excess funds can be reclaimed by contributors)
  5. Funding cycles allow dynamic governance

Successful Juicebox projects:

  • ConstitutionDAO: Raised $47M in 1 week (though lost Constitution auction)
  • AssangeDAO: $53M to support Julian Assange's legal defense
  • MoonDAO: Community-funded space program
  • StudioDAO: Decentralized film financing

Key features:

  • Programmable treasury with built-in governance
  • Overflow protection for contributors
  • NFT rewards for different contribution tiers
  • Funding cycles for iterative development

token_sales.title: Token Sales & Launchpads
token_sales.content:
Token sales let projects raise capital by selling tokens directly to supporters, either through public sales or launchpad platforms.

Sale models:

  • Public sale: Open to anyone, often oversubscribed
  • Whitelist sale: Pre-approved participants, reduces bot activity
  • Dutch auction: Price starts high and descends until clearing
  • Bonding curve: Price increases with each purchase

Launchpad platforms:

  • CoinList: Premier platform, requires compliance, accredited in US
  • Republic Crypto: Reg CF crowdfunding, accessible to retail
  • DAO Maker: Strong holder base (SHO model)
  • Polkastarter: Multi-chain launchpad

Regulatory considerations:

  • US: Difficult due to securities laws, consider excluding US or using Reg D/Reg CF
  • Utility token: If truly decentralized and functional, may not be security
  • SAFT: Helps delay token delivery until network is decentralized
  • Legal counsel: Essential—crypto securities law is complex

investment_daos.title: Investment DAOs
investment_daos.content:
Investment DAOs pool capital from members to invest collectively in crypto projects, often with better terms than retail access.

How they work:

  • Members contribute capital to DAO treasury
  • DAO votes on which projects to invest in
  • DAO receives tokens or equity
  • Returns flow back to DAO members

Types of investment DAOs:

  • Syndicate: Platform for creating investment DAOs with legal structure
  • AngelList Crypto: Rolling funds and syndicates for crypto deals
  • Echo: Community-driven allocation (members can claim portions)
  • MetaCartel Ventures: Early-stage crypto DAO investor

For founders:

  • Investment DAOs can write smaller checks ($25K-$250K) than traditional VCs
  • Often more community-aligned and engaged
  • Can provide grassroots support and evangelism
  • Due diligence process may be longer (requires DAO vote)

For investors:

  • Access to deals typically reserved for VCs
  • Learn by participating in due diligence
  • Diversification across portfolio
  • Regulatory uncertainty (DAO structure in legal gray area)

application_tips.title: Application Tips & Best Practices
application_tips.content: Whether applying for grants or pitching VCs, your application is your first impression. Make it count.

grant_applications.title: Writing Strong Grant Applications
grant_applications.content:
Grant reviewers read dozens or hundreds of applications. Make yours stand out by being clear, specific, and impact-focused.

Essential components:

  • Problem statement: What specific problem are you solving? Why does it matter?
  • Solution: How does your project address this problem uniquely?
  • Impact: Who benefits? How will you measure success?
  • Team: Why are you uniquely qualified? Relevant experience?
  • Milestones: Specific, measurable deliverables with timeline
  • Budget: Transparent breakdown of how funds will be used
  • Prior work: GitHub repos, demos, previous grants, traction

Do:

  • Align with the grant program's stated priorities
  • Provide links to live demos, GitHub, or prototypes
  • Be specific about deliverables (not vague promises)
  • Show you've already started (skin in the game)
  • Explain how this benefits the broader ecosystem, not just your project

Don't:

  • Submit generic applications used for multiple grants
  • Ask for funding without clear milestones
  • Overpromise or present unrealistic timelines
  • Hide team members or stay anonymous (red flag for grants)
  • Ignore the grant's focus areas

pitch_decks.title: Creating Effective Pitch Decks
pitch_decks.content:
VCs see hundreds of decks. Your pitch deck needs to tell a compelling story in 10-15 slides that gets them excited to learn more.

Standard deck structure:

  1. Cover: Name, tagline, logo
  2. Problem: What's broken? Why now?
  3. Solution: Your unique approach
  4. Product: Demo or screenshots
  5. Market: TAM/SAM/SOM, growth trends
  6. Traction: Users, TVL, revenue, growth rate
  7. Token economics: Supply, distribution, utility, value accrual
  8. Roadmap: What you'll build with funding
  9. Team: Founders and key hires, relevant experience
  10. Competition: Landscape and your differentiation
  11. Business model: How you capture value
  12. Fundraise: Amount raising, use of funds, target milestones

Crypto-specific slides to include:

  • Token economics: Critical for VCs evaluating token investments
  • Smart contract audits: If already deployed
  • Governance: How the protocol will be governed
  • Go-to-market: How you'll bootstrap liquidity/users

Design tips:

  • Use high-quality visuals and consistent branding
  • One idea per slide (not walls of text)
  • Lead with data and charts (VCs love metrics)
  • Include founder photos (builds trust)

milestones.title: Setting Achievable Milestones
milestones.content:
Milestones prove you can execute and help funders track progress. They should be specific, measurable, and time-bound.

Good milestones:

  • "Deploy audited smart contracts to mainnet" (specific, verifiable)
  • "Reach $10M TVL" (measurable)
  • "Integrate with 5 DEXs for liquidity aggregation" (specific number)
  • "Launch mobile app on iOS and Android" (clear deliverable)
  • "Publish security audit from Trail of Bits" (specific, verifiable)

Bad milestones:

  • "Build the product" (vague)
  • "Grow the community" (not measurable)
  • "Improve UX" (subjective)
  • "Research solutions" (no concrete output)

Milestone-based funding:

  • Tranche 1 (30%): Initial development and testing
  • Tranche 2 (40%): Mainnet launch and audit
  • Tranche 3 (30%): Growth and ecosystem integration

Reporting:

  • Many grants require monthly or quarterly updates
  • Be transparent about progress and blockers
  • Share links to GitHub commits, deployed contracts, metrics dashboards
  • Public updates build trust and can lead to follow-on funding

building_relationships.title: Building Relationships
building_relationships.content: Fundraising is about relationships, not transactions. The best founders build relationships before they need money.

networking.title: Networking in Crypto
networking.content:
Crypto is a small, tight-knit industry. Your reputation and relationships are your most valuable assets.

Where to network:

  • Conferences: Devcon, ETHDenver, EthCC, Consensus, TOKEN2049
  • Hackathons: ETHGlobal events, Buildathons, chain-specific hackathons
  • Twitter/X: Engage with VCs, builders, and thought leaders
  • Discord/Telegram: Join communities of projects you admire
  • Podcasts: Go on podcasts to share your story
  • Demo days: Accelerator demo days (Alliance, Kernel, Outlier Ventures)

Effective networking strategies:

  • Add value first: Help others before asking for help
  • Be genuinely curious: Learn from others, don't just pitch
  • Follow up: Send a note after meeting someone
  • Stay in touch: Share updates even when not fundraising
  • Be memorable: Have a clear, concise way to explain your project

Building VC relationships:

  • Start conversations before you need funding
  • Share monthly updates (product, metrics, learnings)
  • Ask for advice, not money (at first)
  • Introduce them to other interesting founders
  • When you do fundraise, you'll have warm intros

community_building.title: Community Building
community_building.content:
Your community is your moat. Strong communities lead to better fundraising, user acquisition, and long-term sustainability.

Building from scratch:

  • Start with value: Create useful content, tools, or insights before asking for support
  • Find early believers: 1-on-1 conversations with aligned individuals
  • Create gathering spaces: Discord, Telegram, or forum
  • Engage authentically: Founders should be active in the community
  • Recognize contributors: Highlight and reward community members

Community-led funding:

  • Gitcoin Grants: Small donors get matched quadratically (favors broad support)
  • Mirror crowdfunds: Writing NFTs for funding
  • Juicebox: Community treasury with contributor governance
  • Community rounds: Allocate token sale slots to community before VC rounds

Long-term community value:

  • Community members become evangelists
  • Early supporters provide feedback and bug reports
  • Community growth attracts VC interest
  • Decentralized ownership creates resilience

public_goods.title: Building Public Goods
public_goods.content:
Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable—anyone can use them without diminishing others' access. They're chronically underfunded in traditional markets but thrive in crypto thanks to retroactive funding and grants.

Examples of crypto public goods:

  • Infrastructure: RPC nodes, indexers, archive nodes
  • Developer tools: Libraries, testing frameworks, boilerplate code
  • Standards: ERCs, protocol specifications
  • Education: Tutorials, documentation, translations
  • Research: Academic papers, mechanism design
  • Audits & security: Open-source audit reports, security tooling

Why build public goods:

  • Retroactive funding: Optimism RetroPGF, Gitcoin, others reward impact after the fact
  • Grants: Easier to get grants for public goods than commercial products
  • Reputation: Building respected public goods establishes you as a leader
  • Network effects: Your tool gets adopted widely, creating moats

Sustainability models:

  • Grants: Continuous funding from ecosystems
  • Retroactive funding: Periodic rounds reward past impact
  • Freemium: Free open-source + paid hosted/support tiers
  • DAO ownership: Governance token for community funding

Philosophy: "Build public goods, get rewarded retroactively" is a powerful new model. Don't wait for upfront funding—build something valuable, demonstrate impact, and funding will follow.

grant.definition: Non-dilutive funding provided to projects, typically focused on public goods, infrastructure, or ecosystem development. Unlike VC funding, grants don't require giving up equity or tokens.

retroactive_funding.definition: Funding model that rewards projects after they've demonstrated impact, rather than predicting future success. Popularized by Optimism's RetroPGF program.

quadratic_funding.definition: Democratic funding mechanism where matching funds are allocated based on the number of contributors, not just the amount. Smaller donations from more people receive larger matches than large donations from few people.

safe.definition: Investment contract where investors provide capital in exchange for the right to receive equity at a future date, typically at a discount. In crypto, SAFT (Simple Agreement for Future Tokens) is the token equivalent.

valuation.definition: The estimated worth of a project or protocol. In crypto, typically measured as FDV (Fully Diluted Valuation) = token price × total supply, even if tokens aren't yet circulating.

runway.definition: The amount of time a project can operate before running out of funds, calculated as: current funds ÷ monthly burn rate. Example: $500K in bank, $50K/month burn = 10 months runway.

milestone.definition: Specific, measurable goals that a project commits to achieving, often tied to funding tranches. Good milestones are concrete (e.g., 'deploy audited contracts to mainnet') not vague (e.g., 'improve product').

treasury.definition: The funds controlled by a DAO or protocol, typically held in a multisig or governed by token holders. Used for grants, development, partnerships, and ecosystem growth.

dao_grants.definition: Grants funded and governed by DAOs using their treasuries. Examples include Uniswap Grants, Aave Grants, and Compound Grants, where token holders vote on allocations.

public_goods.definition: Products or services that are non-rival (one person's use doesn't reduce availability) and non-excludable (can't prevent others from using). Examples: open-source code, documentation, research.
